title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 889–890 (Night 213, continuing nights-212), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 213 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. In the gardener's orchard he watches the two mourning birds bury their dead companion, fly off and come back with the killer, and tear it apart over the grave. Where the bird was killed he finds its crop, and inside it the stone that parted him from his wife; he faints for joy, takes it for a sign that they will meet again, and ties it to his arm. The gardener does not come back that night. In the morning, digging round a carob tree, Qamar al-Zamān hears his axe ring, clears away the earth and finds a trapdoor; and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّالِثَةَ عَشَرَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thālithata ʿashara baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the thirteenth after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and thirteenth night,
sentences.n: al-thālithata ʿashara, “thirteenth”: as in the nights before, the print has عشر where Classical Arabic would make the second part feminine (ʿashrata) to agree with the night; it is vocalised as printed. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ بَكَى عَلَى فِرَاقِ زَوْجَتِهِ وَوَالِدِهِ حِينَ رَأَى الطَّائِرَيْنِ يَبْكِيَانِ عَلَى صَاحِبِهِمَا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Qamara al-Zamāni bakā ʿalā firāqi zawjatihi wa-wālidihi ḥīna raʾā al-ṭāʾirayni yabkiyāni ʿalā ṣāḥibihimā
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān wept over (the) parting (of) his-wife and-his-father, when he-saw the-two-birds weeping over their-companion.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān wept for the loss of his wife and of his father when he saw the two birds weeping over their companion.
sentences.n: The night takes up the last sentence of the one before, with a small difference: there he wept for his wife and remembered his father; here both hang on firāq, “parting from his wife and his father”. Qamara is accusative after anna. bakā ʿalā, “to weep over”: ʿalā marks what is mourned. wālidihi, “his father”, is genitive, joined by wa- to zawjatihi. yabkiyāni, dual, “the two of them weeping”, describes the birds as he saw them. The hamza of رأى and the ئ of الطائرين are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ نَظَرَ إِلَى الطَّائِرَيْنِ فَرَآهُمَا قَدْ حَفَرَا حُفْرَةً وَدَفَنَا الطَّائِرَ الْمَقْتُولَ فِيهَا
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni naẓara ilā al-ṭāʾirayni fa-raʾāhumā qad ḥafarā ḥufratan wa-dafanā al-ṭāʾira al-maqtūla fīhā
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān looked to the-two-birds, and-he-saw-them-two: already they-two-had-dug a-pit and-they-two-had-buried the-bird the-slain in-it.
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān looked at the two birds and saw that they had dug a hole and buried the slain bird in it.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then”, the narrator's turn to the next event: Qamara is accusative after inna. naẓara ilā, “to look at”: ilā marks what is looked at. raʾāhumā qad ḥafarā, “he saw them, they having dug”: the clause with qad tells what he saw them do. ḥafarā and dafanā are dual verbs, “the two of them”. ḥufra, “pit, hole”, from the same root as ḥafara, “to dig”. The madda of فرآهما and the ئ of الطائرين and الطائر are printed.

sentences.t: وَطَارَا إِلَى الْجَوِّ وَغَابَا سَاعَةً ثُمَّ عَادَا وَمَعَهُمَا الطَّائِرُ الْقَاتِلُ فَنَزَلَا بِهِ عَلَى قَبْرِ الْمَقْتُولِ
sentences.tr: wa-ṭārā ilā al-jawwi wa-ghābā sāʿatan thumma ʿādā wa-maʿahumā al-ṭāʾiru al-qātilu fa-nazalā bihi ʿalā qabri al-maqtūli
sentences.l: And-they-two-flew to the-sky and-they-two-were-gone an-hour; then they-two-returned, and-with-them-two the-bird the-killer, and-they-two-came-down with-it upon (the) grave (of) the-slain-one.
sentences.i: Then they flew up into the sky and were gone for a while; and they came back bringing the bird that had done the killing, and came down with it upon the dead bird's grave.
sentences.n: ṭāra ilā, “to fly up to”: ilā marks where; the shadda of الجوّ is printed. sāʿatan, “an hour”, that is, a while: an accusative of time. wa-maʿahumā al-ṭāʾiru al-qātilu, “and with them (was) the killer bird”, a circumstantial clause. nazala bi-, “to come down with”: bi- marks what is brought down. The ئ of الطائر is printed.

sentences.t: وَبَرَكَا عَلَى الْقَاتِلِ حَتَّى قَتَلَاهُ وَشَقَّا جَوْفَهُ وَأَخْرَجَا أَمْعَاءَهُ وَأَرَاقَا دَمَهُ عَلَى قَبْرِ الطَّائِرِ الْمَقْتُولِ
sentences.tr: wa-barakā ʿalā al-qātili ḥattā qatalāhu wa-shaqqā jawfahu wa-akhrajā amʿāʾahu wa-arāqā damahu ʿalā qabri al-ṭāʾiri al-maqtūli
sentences.l: And-they-two-knelt upon the-killer until they-two-killed-him, and-they-two-split his-belly, and-they-two-brought-out his-guts, and-they-two-poured-out his-blood upon (the) grave (of) the-bird the-slain.
sentences.i: They bore down upon the killer until they had killed it; then they split open its belly, pulled out its entrails, and poured out its blood on the grave of the slain bird.
sentences.n: The print has امعاءة, a misprint for امعاءه, corrected here. baraka ʿalā, “to kneel upon”, properly of a camel couching, here to pin down with the whole weight: ʿalā marks the one pinned. shaqqa, “to split”; the shadda of وشقّا is printed. jawf, “belly, inside”. amʿāʾ, “guts”, plural of miʿan; the hamza of امعاءه is printed. arāqa, Form IV, “to pour out, shed”. The ئ of الطائر is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَثَرَا لَحْمَهُ وَمَزَّقَا جِلْدَهُ وَأَخْرَجَا مَا فِي جَوْفِهِ وَفَرَّقَاهُ إِلَى أَمَاكِنَ مُتَفَرِّقَةٍ
sentences.tr: thumma natharā laḥmahu wa-mazzaqā jildahu wa-akhrajā mā fī jawfihi wa-farraqāhu ilā amākina mutafarriqatin
sentences.l: Then they-two-scattered its-flesh, and-they-two-tore-up its-skin, and-they-two-brought-out what (was) in its-belly, and-they-two-dispersed-it to places scattered.
sentences.i: Then they scattered its flesh, tore its skin to shreds, took out what was inside it, and strewed it about in places far apart.
sentences.n: The print has جلدة, a misprint for جلده, corrected here. nathara, “to scatter, strew”. mazzaqa, Form II, “to tear to pieces”; its shadda is printed. farraqa ilā, Form II, “to divide out, distribute to”: ilā marks where the pieces go. mutafarriqa, “scattered, separate”, from Form V of the same root; its shadda is printed. amākin, plural of makān, “place”, is a diptote: after ilā it takes -a and no tanwīn.

sentences.t: هٰذَا كُلُّهُ جَرَى وَقَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ يَنْظُرُ وَيَتَعَجَّبُ
sentences.tr: hādhā kulluhu jarā wa-Qamaru al-Zamāni yanẓuru wa-yataʿajjabu
sentences.l: This, all-of-it, happened, and-Qamar al-Zamān (was) looking and-marvelling.
sentences.i: All this took place while Qamar al-Zamān looked on in wonder.
sentences.n: hādhā kulluhu, “this, all of it”, is put first for emphasis; jarā, “to run”, here “to happen, take place”. wa-Qamaru al-Zamāni yanẓuru, “while Qamar al-Zamān was looking”, a circumstantial clause opened by wa-. taʿajjaba, Form V, “to wonder, marvel”; its shadda is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَاحَتْ مِنْهُ الْتِفَاتَةٌ إِلَى الْمَوْضِعِ الَّذِي قَتَلَا فِيهِ الطَّائِرَ فَوَجَدَ شَيْأً يَلْمَعُ
sentences.tr: fa-lāḥat minhu iltifātatun ilā al-mawḍiʿi alladhī qatalā fīhi al-ṭāʾira fa-wajada shayʾan yalmaʿu
sentences.l: And-appeared from-him a-turning-glance to the-place which they-two-killed in-it the-bird, and-he-found a-thing gleaming.
sentences.i: Then he chanced to glance towards the spot where they had killed the bird, and saw something glittering there.
sentences.n: lāḥat minhu iltifātatun ilā, “a turning (of the head) showed itself from him towards”, a set phrase for a chance glance: min marks the one who glances, ilā where he looks. alladhī qatalā fīhi, “in which they killed”: fīhi, “in it”, points back to the place. The print spells شيأ, with the hamza on an alif, where Classical Arabic writes شيئا; it is read shayʾan, and the hamza is printed. lamaʿa, “to gleam, glitter”: yalmaʿu describes the thing. The ئ of الطائر is printed.

sentences.t: فَدَنَى مِنْهُ فَوَجَدَهُ حَوْصَلَةَ الطَّائِرِ فَأَخَذَهَا وَفَتَحَهَا فَوَجَدَ فِيهَا الْفَصَّ الَّذِي كَانَ سَبَبَ فِرَاقِهِ مِنْ زَوْجَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-danā minhu fa-wajadahu ḥawṣalata al-ṭāʾiri fa-akhadhahā wa-fataḥahā fa-wajada fīhā al-faṣṣa alladhī kāna sababa firāqihi min zawjatihi
sentences.l: And-he-drew-near to-it, and-he-found-it (the) crop (of) the-bird; and-he-took-it and-opened-it, and-he-found in-it the-stone which was (the) cause (of) his-parting from his-wife.
sentences.i: He went up to it and found that it was the bird's crop. He took it and opened it, and inside he found the stone that had been the cause of his parting from his wife.
sentences.n: The print has فوجدة, a misprint for فوجده, corrected here. The print spells فدنى with ى, where Classical Arabic writes دنا; read danā. danā min, “to draw near to”: min marks what is approached. wajadahu ḥawṣalata al-ṭāʾiri, “he found it (to be) the bird's crop”: wajada takes two accusatives, the thing and what it proves to be. ḥawṣala, “crop, craw”, the pouch in a bird's gullet. al-faṣṣ, “the stone” of the earlier nights, a gem set in a ring or worn as a charm. firāq min, “parting from”: min marks the one he was parted from. The ئ of الطائر is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهُ وَعَرَفَهُ وَقَعَ عَلَي الْأَرْضِ مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهِ مِنْ فَرْحَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhu wa-ʿarafahu waqaʿa ʿalā al-arḍi maghshiyyan ʿalayhi min farḥatihi
sentences.l: And-when he-saw-it and-knew-it, he-fell upon the-ground, fainted-upon-him, from his-joy.
sentences.i: When he saw it and knew it for what it was, he fell to the ground in a swoon for very joy.
sentences.n: The print has رآة, a misprint for رآه, corrected here; the madda is printed. The print spells علي with ي where Classical Arabic writes على; read ʿalā. maghshiyyan ʿalayhi, “swooning”, literally “fainted upon”: the passive participle of ghashiya, a circumstantial accusative, with ʿalā marking the one who swoons. farḥa, “joy”: min gives the cause, “out of joy”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَفَاقَ قَالَ الْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهِ هٰذِهِ عَلَامَةُ الْخَيْرِ وَبِشَارَةُ الِاجْتِمَاعِ بِمَحْبُوبَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā afāqa qāla al-ḥamdu li-llāhi hādhihi ʿalāmatu al-khayri wa-bishāratu al-ijtimāʿi bi-maḥbūbatī
sentences.l: And-when he-came-to, he-said: The-praise (is) to-God! This (is the) sign (of) the-good and-(the)-glad-tidings (of) the-meeting with-my-beloved.
sentences.i: When he came to himself he said, “Praise be to God! This is a sign of good fortune, and glad tidings that I shall be united with my beloved.”
sentences.n: The print has هذة, a misprint for هذه, corrected here. afāqa, Form IV, “to come to oneself”. al-ḥamdu li-llāhi, “praise (be) to God”: li- marks the one to whom praise belongs. ʿalāmat al-khayr, “a sign of good”, a good omen. bishāra, “glad tidings”. al-ijtimāʿ bi-, “coming together with, union with”: bi- marks the one he will be with. maḥbūba, “beloved (f.)”, the passive participle of ḥabba, “to love” (the commoner verb is Form IV aḥabba).

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَأَمَّلَهُ وَمَرَّبِهِ عَلَى عَيْنِهِ وَرَبَطَهُ عَلَى ذِرَاعِهِ وَاسْتَبْشَرَ بِالْخَيْرِ
sentences.tr: thumma taʾammalahu wa-marra bihi ʿalā ʿaynihi wa-rabaṭahu ʿalā dhirāʿihi wa-istabshara bi-al-khayri
sentences.l: Then he-gazed-at-it, and-passed it over his-eye, and-tied-it upon his-arm, and-took-glad-heart at-the-good.
sentences.i: Then he gazed at it long, passed it over his eyes, and tied it upon his arm, taking heart at the good omen.
sentences.n: taʾammala, Form V, “to look closely at, contemplate”; its hamza and shadda are printed. The print sets ومرّبه as one word, wa-marra bihi; it is kept as set, and the shadda is printed. marra bi- … ʿalā, “to pass (something) over”: bi- marks the thing moved, as the verb requires, and ʿalā what it passes over; to touch the eyes with a cherished thing is a gesture of love and thanks. rabaṭa ʿalā, “to tie on”: ʿalā marks where. istabshara bi-, Form X, “to take heart at good news”: bi- marks what gladdens him.

sentences.t: وَقَامَ يَتَمَشَّى يَنْتَظِرُ الْخَوْلِيَّ إِلَى اللَّيْلِ فَلَمْ يَأْتِ فَبَاتَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ فِي مَوْضِعِهِ إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāma yatamashshā yantaẓiru al-khawliyya ilā al-layli fa-lam yaʾti fa-bāta Qamaru al-Zamāni fī mawḍiʿihi ilā al-ṣabāḥi
sentences.l: And-he-rose walking-about, waiting-for the-gardener until the-night; and-not he-came, and-passed-the-night Qamar al-Zamān in his-place until the-morning.
sentences.i: He got up and walked about, waiting for the gardener until nightfall; but he did not come, and Qamar al-Zamān spent the night where he was until morning.
sentences.n: qāma yatamashshā yantaẓiru, “he rose, walking about, waiting”: the two imperfects tell what he did after rising; the shadda of يتمشّى is printed. al-khawlī, “the gardener”, an Egyptian word. ilā al-layli, “until night”: ilā marks the limit of time. lam yaʾti, “he did not come”: the jussive of atā after lam, its final vowel cut short; the hamza is printed. bāta, “to spend the night”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَ إِلَى شُغْلِهِ وَشَدَّ وَسَطَهُ بِحَبْلٍ مِنَ اللِّيفِ وَأَخَذَ الْفَأْسَ وَالْقُفَّةَ وَشَقَّ فِى الْبُسْتَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma qāma ilā shughlihi wa-shadda wasaṭahu bi-ḥablin mina al-līfi wa-akhadha al-faʾsa wa-al-quffata wa-shaqqa fī al-bustāni
sentences.l: Then he-rose to his-work, and-bound his-middle with-a-rope of the-palm-fibre, and-took the-axe and-the-basket, and-cut-through in the-garden.
sentences.i: Then he rose and went to his work. He girded his waist with a rope of palm fibre, took up the axe and the basket, and made his way through the orchard.
sentences.n: qāma ilā, “to rise (and go) to”: ilā marks the goal. shughl, “work, task”. shadda … bi-, “to bind with”: bi- marks the means; the shadda of وشدّ is printed. min al-līfi, “of palm fibre”: min marks the stuff the rope is made of. The print spells الفاس, and we supply the hamza, al-faʾs, “axe”, as in the nights before; in the garden it is the heavy hoe or mattock, and Middle Arabic said fās. quffa, “basket”, the palm-leaf basket for carrying earth; its shadda is printed. shaqqa fī, “to cut through, make one's way through”: fī marks the ground crossed; the shadda of وشقّ is printed, and فى is spelt with ى.

sentences.t: فَأَتَي إِلَى شَجَرَةِ خَرُّوبٍ وَضَرَبَ الْفَأْسَ فِي جِدْرِهَا فَطَنَّتِ الضَّرْبَةُ فَكَشَفَ التُّرَابَ عَنْ مَوْضِعِهَا فَوَجَدَ طَابَقًا فَفَتَحَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-atā ilā shajarati kharrūbin wa-ḍaraba al-faʾsa fī jidrihā fa-ṭannati al-ḍarbatu fa-kashafa al-turāba ʿan mawḍiʿihā fa-wajada ṭābaqan fa-fataḥahu
sentences.l: And-he-came to a-tree (of) carob, and-struck the-axe into its-root, and-rang the-blow; and-he-uncovered the-earth from its-place, and-he-found a-trapdoor, and-he-opened-it.
sentences.i: He came to a carob tree and drove the axe into its root, and the blow rang out. So he cleared the earth away from the spot, and found a trapdoor, and opened it.
sentences.n: The print spells فاتي with ي, where Classical Arabic writes فأتى; read fa-atā, “and he came”. atā ilā, “to come to”: ilā marks the goal. kharrūb, “carob”. ḍaraba al-faʾsa fī, “to strike the axe into”: fī marks what it bites into. The print has جدرها, which we vocalise jidrihā and read as “its root, its stump”, as in the night before: it may be meant for jidhr (جذر), the Classical word, which the spoken language says with d; the reading is likely but not certain. ṭanna, “to ring, resound”, as metal does on something hollow; its shadda is printed, and the feminine verb agrees with al-ḍarba, “the blow”. kashafa … ʿan, “to clear (something) away from”: the object, al-turāb, is what is removed, and ʿan marks the place laid bare; -hā in mawḍiʿihā points back to the blow (or the tree), the spot where it rang. ṭābaq, “a lid, a flat cover over an opening”, here a trapdoor in the ground; a word of the later language.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ. Here the print sets the name as one word, شهرزاد.
